analysis.one_liner: India's largest airline by domestic market share, flying an almost entirely leased Airbus narrow-body fleet, now adding Airbus A350 wide-bodies from 2027 to build an international long-haul network.
analysis.whats_happening: Q2 FY27 (quarter ended Sept 2026) results, reported around Oct 29, 2026 - just before this report - showed another large net loss (cited as ₹1,879 crore by one source and ₹2,055 crore by another; not fully reconciled, direction agreed), even as revenue grew. New CEO Willie Walsh, who took charge in August 2026 after Pieter Elbers resigned, warned of further fare hikes to offset sharply higher fuel costs. This followed a disruptive year: a December 2025 scheduling crisis caused thousands of cancellations and a DGCA-mandated 10% winter capacity cut, and FY26 ended with a full-year net loss of roughly ₹2,400 crore.
analysis.plain_terms: IndiGo carries more domestic passengers than any other Indian airline, and that business keeps growing. But it has lost money in most of the last several quarters - not because fewer people are flying, but because of costs it doesn't fully control: a weaker rupee inflating dollar-denominated aircraft lease payments, rising fuel prices, and a long-running grounding of planes with faulty Pratt & Whitney engines that forces it to pay extra for substitute aircraft. On top of that, a scheduling failure in December 2025 caused mass cancellations and a regulatory penalty. The tension: dominant market position and growing revenue, but unpredictable accounting profit and two execution stumbles in two years.
analysis.quarters: The last five reported quarters have been volatile. Q2 FY26 (Sept 2025): revenue up 9.3% YoY to ₹18,555 crore, but a reported net loss of about ₹2,582 crore once forex mark-to-market losses on dollar lease liabilities are included - management separately disclosed a small ₹104 crore profit 'ex-forex', so this was largely a currency-translation loss, not a collapse in ticket sales. Q3 FY26 (Dec 2025): profit fell 78% YoY to about ₹550 crore, hit by new labour-code costs and roughly ₹550 crore of direct costs from that quarter's cancellation crisis. Q4 FY26 (March 2026): a loss near ₹2,660 crore. Q1 FY27 (June 2026) and Q2 FY27 (Sept 2026, latest): both losses, with fuel costs cited as rising as much as 86% YoY in one quarter, far outpacing revenue growth. Exact figures for the two most recent quarters differ across sources and are not fully reconciled - treat as approximate pending the official filing.
analysis.performance_read: No split, bonus or demerger affects this stock's price history, so the ~21% fall from the August 2025 peak (₹6,155.5) to the current ₹4,877.6 is a genuine market reassessment, not a statistical artifact. Over 1 year the stock is down 14.8% against the Nifty's 10.9% fall - recent underperformance. But over 3 years it is up 99% versus the Nifty's 21%, and over 5 years up 124% versus 29% - a large long-term outperformer built on post-Covid domestic dominance. The last year's weakness lines up with real operating setbacks (engine grounding, the December 2025 crisis, a CEO transition), not a narrative-only correction.
analysis.valuation_read: P/E isn't meaningful right now because trailing earnings are a loss. P/B of roughly 47x looks extreme, but that's largely structural - IndiGo's book equity is small because of a large pre-IPO dividend in 2015 that pushed net worth negative, combined with an asset-light, mostly-leased fleet. ROCE is low (under 5%), reflecting the recent loss-making run. The more relevant yardstick for a lease-heavy airline, EV/EBITDAR, puts IndiGo near 13x by one broker estimate - well above global peers such as Ryanair, IAG or Southwest, which trade around 4-7x EV/EBITDA. So it is expensive relative to global peers, and that premium is a bet on continued domestic scale and international expansion, not a reflection of current profitability.
analysis.growth_read: Revenue is still growing and this is volume-led: FY26 capacity (ASK) guidance was raised to 'early teens' percentage growth, international routes have grown faster than domestic (over 26% YoY in one recent quarter) as part of a plan to take international to roughly 40% of capacity by FY30, backed by a firm order for 60 A350 wide-bodies (deliveries from 2027). Margins have moved the opposite way - squeezed, not expanded, by fuel and forex costs. The complication: the Pratt & Whitney engine-grounding issue, guided down to 'sub-40' aircraft by April 2026, was instead reported near 64 grounded aircraft later in 2026, so growth is running into a capacity constraint that hasn't resolved on schedule.
analysis.health_read: The underlying business generates real cash from ticket sales - domestic volumes and revenue kept growing through the past year - but reported accounting profit has not tracked it. The losses trace to rupee-driven forex translation on dollar lease liabilities, new labour-code costs, direct costs of the December 2025 cancellation crisis, and sharply higher fuel prices. That points to financial/input-cost exposure (currency, fuel) layered on top of execution risk (the self-inflicted scheduling failure and the slower-than-guided engine fix), rather than weak underlying demand. Total debt including lease liabilities is large (reported between roughly ₹77,000-92,000 crore depending on definition), but a chunk of that reflects lease accounting on an all-leased fleet rather than conventional borrowing.
analysis.ownership_read: Promoter holding is 41.57% with zero shares pledged - clean on paper. But it is split between two founders: InterGlobe Enterprises (Rahul Bhatia side) holds the bulk, around 35.7%, while co-founder Rakesh Gangwal's family has been steadily exiting since announcing a 2022 wind-down plan - down from about 13.5% in early 2025 to roughly 4.78% now, with cumulative sale proceeds reported near ₹45,300 crore. Foreign institutional holding has fallen to a multi-year low (around 20%) while domestic institutions have risen to a record high (around 33%), largely absorbing the shares Gangwal has sold.
strengths: Domestic market leadership intact with revenue still growing - Q2 FY26 revenue up 9.3% YoY to ₹18,555 crore despite the engine-grounding disruption
Promoter stake of 41.57% carries zero pledge, an unencumbered ownership base
3-year and 5-year shareholder returns of 99% and 124% have comfortably beaten the Nifty's 21% and 29% over the same periods
60 A350 wide-bodies on firm order for international long-haul, with international capacity already growing over 26% YoY in a recent quarter
watchpoints: Four of the last five reported quarters have shown net losses, with the exact size of the most recent loss unreconciled across sources (₹1,879-2,055 crore) - confirm against the official filing before relying on it
Pratt & Whitney engine grounding was guided down to 'sub-40' aircraft by April 2026 but was reported near 64 aircraft later in the year - the fix is running behind schedule

December 2025 scheduling crisis (thousands of cancellations, a DGCA-mandated 10% winter capacity cut, a show-cause notice) was attributed to internal planning failure around new pilot duty-time rules, and preceded a 2026 CEO change
Fuel costs rose as much as 86% YoY in one quarter, prompting fare and fuel-surcharge hikes (most recently October 2026) - margin recovery depends on passing these costs through without losing share
analysis.one_thing: Whether the count of Pratt & Whitney-grounded aircraft actually falls toward management's guided range and quarterly profit (ex-forex) turns consistent again - watch the Q3 FY27 (December 2026 quarter) results, expected around late January 2027.
analysis.data_notes: Revenue and EBITDAR figures for FY26 quarters were cross-checked across company press releases and Business Standard and were consistent. Net loss figures for the two most recent quarters (Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27) and the FY26 full-year loss could not be fully reconciled between aggregator (Screener) and press-report (Business Standard, Outlook India) figures - treated as approximate ranges. Debt including lease liabilities varied by definition across sources (~₹77,000-92,000 crore). ROE was found at both -30.2% and +25.47% depending on snapshot date and is too volatile quarter-to-quarter to state as one figure, so it was omitted. Promoter holding (41.57%, 0% pledge) was the most consistently corroborated ownership figure; FII/DII/public splits showed minor cross-source inconsistencies.
